# SK2132 — The accessor uses another property's backing field

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A property that has a conventionally named backing field of its own reads or writes a different field — one that conventionally backs another property of the same type.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S4275 |

## Why

The copy-paste defect in hand-written properties: the second property is written by duplicating the first and one of the two field names is not changed. It is silent in every direction — the type compiles, the property runs, the getter returns somebody else's value and the setter writes over it — and a test that exercises one property at a time can pass while both are wrong. ⚠ **The reason this needs a rule at all is that nothing else looks**: the compiler has no opinion about which field an accessor reaches for, and a reviewer reading two nearly identical five-line properties is reading exactly the shape human attention is worst at.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Contact {
    string firstName = "";
    string lastName = "";

    public string FirstName {
        get => firstName;
        set => firstName = value;
    }

    public string LastName {
        get => firstName;          // returns the first name
        set => lastName = value;
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Contact {
    string firstName = "";
    string lastName = "";

    public string FirstName {
        get => firstName;
        set => firstName = value;
    }

    public string LastName {
        get => lastName;
        set => lastName = value;
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A name match between a property and a field is a convention, not a fact, and a great deal of correct code breaks it deliberately** — `Count` over `_items` and `Value` over `_inner` are ordinary indirection. A rule that treated "this accessor touches a field that is not named after me" as the finding would report both, so **two conditions must hold together, and they are conditions about two properties rather than one**: the property being examined must itself have a conventionally named field of *exactly its own type* — which puts `Count` over `_items` out, because no `_count` exists — and the field the accessor actually touches must be the conventionally named field of a **different property of the same type** — which puts `_inner` behind `Value` out unless there is also an `Inner` property, at which point the two names have been crossed rather than chosen. The accepted spellings are `_name`, `name`, `m_name` and `_Name` for a property `Name`; a field whose staticness differs from the property's, and a `const`, are never candidates. ⚠ **The type equality is load-bearing rather than tidiness**: without it a `List<string> _name` behind a `string Name` would count as the property's own field and the fix would propose text that does not compile. ⚠ **The accessor must be nothing but the field access** — `get => _items.Count;`, and a getter that logs before returning, are declined by the shape test rather than by a list of exceptions, because the moment an accessor does something in addition to reaching for storage, what it reaches for is a decision rather than a name that was mistyped. `this._name` is accepted as the same shape as `_name`; a setter must be exactly `field = value`, so a setter that transforms `value` is out. The fix rewrites the field reference to the property's own field and is **not** marked safe: it is the one repair in this batch that changes what the program computes, which is the whole point of the finding, and the author may equally have meant to rename the property. Generated code is excluded.
